1.pericope_label: When the LORD thy God hath cut off the nations, thou shalt separate three cities for thee in the midst of thy land; thou shalt prepare thee a way, and divide the coasts of thy land into three parts, that every slayer may flee thither

schools.summary: Set the law under the Noahic precept that the shedder of blood shall have his own blood shed, and read the prepared roads typologically: Christ is no refuge at a distance, and gospel ministers must point the way and clear the obstacles as the messengers cleared the highways.

Ground the gift of the land in God's right to dispose of what he owns and the destruction of the seven nations in their own sin; and locate the exempting principle in the will alone, so that where there is no malicious feeling there is no crime, prior hatred being the test and the inquiry superfluous where a drawn sword was used.

Treat the chapter as a deliberate turn from the national constitution to the endangering of individual life, and the statute as not a repetition of the earlier legislation but an admonition to execute it, extended westward and supplemented with directions for maintaining the roads.
Attend to the practical mechanics — roads thirty-two cubits broad, level and kept in repair, distinguished by evident marks so that mistakes and delays should not cost a life.

debates: Whether the chapter merely repeats the earlier legislation on the cities of refuge or admonishes Israel to execute it with a view to future enlargement (Keil, for the latter).
outliers: Henry alone allegorises the prepared road, making the highway to the city of refuge a figure of gospel ministry.

4.pericope_label: Whoso killeth his neighbour ignorantly, whom he hated not in time past, as when the head slippeth from the helve, he shall flee unto one of those cities and live; but if any man hate his neighbour and lie in wait for him, the elders of his city shall fetch him thence

schools.summary: Read the wood as a public place open alike to him that hurts and him that is hurt, so that the venue itself is part of the test of innocence, and take the eye that may not pity as the magistrate's rather than the avenger's, forbidding favour to citizen, kinsman, friend or rich man.

Insist that the free cities were never asyla for those deserving death, and resist the critical inference that the elders here acquire a judicial function the earlier legislation withheld; they act simply as magistrates of local affairs.

Take the enlargement to Euphrates as genuinely conditional, and, granting with the Jewish writers that the condition failed and the three further cities were never needed, find the promise fulfilled spiritually in the enlarged borders of the gospel Israel rather than deferred to a literal messianic age.

debates: Whether the elders who fetch the murderer out conduct a judicial inquiry — asserted by Riehm after Vater and De Wette to expose a discrepancy with the earlier law, denied by Keil, who confines them to their ordinary magistracy.
Whether the promised enlargement of the coast awaits a literal messianic fulfilment, as the Jewish writers held, or is spiritually fulfilled in the borders of the gospel Israel (Wesley).
outliers: Clarke alone reaches outside Israel, noting the heathen asyla and the Catholic privileged altars as imitations of the cities of refuge.

14.pericope_label: Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour’s landmark, which they of old time have set in thine inheritance; one witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, but at the mouth of two witnesses, or of three witnesses, shall the matter be established

schools.summary: Take the landmark law as a moral precept still binding, and expand it from boundary stones to deeds and writings, to the sowing of discord and manufacture of lawsuits, and to the overturning of ancient usage without cause; and read the two-witness rule as a mercy toward the accused, whose life and honour must not hang on one man's grudge.

Class removal of a landmark as theft — the act itself convicting the mover, since it disturbs a lawful owner in quiet possession, and doubling the crime by concealment — so that those who unjustly possess a neighbour's land stand with those who pillage his cellars.

Supply the antiquarian setting: property once marked by movable stones, the Roman termini held sacred and at last deified with offerings of cakes, lambs, flowers and annual oblations, and the digests vague on penalty though slaves who moved a mark with evil design were put to death.

Note that the landmark law appears here for the first time and that its connection with what precedes is not obvious, deny any idea of antiquity in “they of old time,” and observe that the two-witness rule, once confined to capital crimes, is here raised into a law of general application.

debates: Why the landmark law stands in this context at all: Ellicott finds the connection not obvious and suggests a caution against an incentive to hatred and murder, while Keil rejects the view of Clericus and Rosenmüller that landmarks bore on the manslayer’s flight, grounding it instead in the tie between a man’s property and his life.
outliers: Clarke alone documents the Roman cult of the termini from Ovid, Tibullus and Juvenal; Calvin’s block on this verse carries an editorial footnote reproducing Clarke’s digest note verbatim, so the two agree here by transmission rather than by independent judgement.

16.pericope_label: If a false witness rise up against any man to testify against him that which is wrong, then both the men between whom the controversy is shall stand before the LORD, before the priests and the judges; and the judges shall make diligent inquisition

schools.summary: Fix the venue at the sanctuary rather than the local courts, read the clauses about the witness as parenthetical and circumstantial, gloss the verb of intention as meditating evil, and note from Diodorus that Egypt punished false accusers by the same rule.

Press the thoroughness of the examination, with the Targum having the judges interrogate the witness well; and explain the penalty from the state of men, since the fear of God does not restrain all from slander, so that false witnesses and murderers stand in the same light before God and the presence of the priests marks a demand for unusual diligence.
Mark the asymmetry that makes the statute work: one truthful witness cannot condemn another man, yet one conviction of falsehood suffices to condemn the witness himself.

debates: Whether the parties came before the central tribunal at the sanctuary (Keil) or before the local courts (Knobel).

Whether perjury could be tried without an accuser: Calvin grants that the statute supposes a complaint, but holds that reason requires official inquiry where a man has been put to death on false testimony.
outliers: Calvin alone asks why a penal statute is needed at all, and answers from the insufficiency of the fear of God in most men.

19.pericope_label: Then shall ye do unto him as he had thought to have done unto his brother; and those which remain shall hear, and fear; and thine eye shall not pity, but life shall go for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth

schools.summary: State the rule of reciprocity plainly and then widen it, finding the same principle in English statutes of Edward the Third and in the Twelve Tables, and defending penal provision as necessary to civil society even while granting that a Christian may forgive private injuries where the public peace is not touched.

Enumerate the possible penalties the false witness incurs, note the rabbinic qualification that an accuser of a priest's daughter was strangled rather than burnt, and read the retaliation clause in the received Jewish sense as the price of an eye for an eye.

debates: How far the retaliation clause is to be taken literally: Gill reports the received Jewish sense of the price of a member, while Clarke wishes the law itself still in force.
outliers: Clarke alone distinguishes the Christian’s liberty to forgive private injury from the magistrate’s duty to punish, holding that without the latter civil society would be destroyed.
